explanations.explanation: His friends take the ship, and Paul takes his own two feet. Verse 13 says he arranged it that way because he was going there on foot. Then he meets them at Assos and they take him aboard (Acts 20:14). I think that's a man who knew exactly where he'd be standing when the boat pulled in.

explanations.answer: He rides there on a donkey
explanations.explanation: A donkey would make a fun picture, I'll give you that. But the text never mentions one. It says Paul arranged for his friends to take the ship ahead, because he was going to Assos on foot. Just Paul and the road.

explanations.answer: He sails there on another ship
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, since everybody else is on a ship. But the writer says his group went ahead to the ship and sailed to Assos to take Paul aboard there. So Paul isn't on a ship yet. He's on foot, and they pick him up when he arrives (Acts 20:13-14).

Verse 16 says Paul was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost. That's why he decided to sail past Ephesus. He didn't want to spend time in the province of Asia. I'd say that's a man watching the calendar, friend.
Rome is a big name, but it isn't in this passage. The text says Paul wanted to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost. That's the deadline he's racing, and winter never comes up.
Good guess for a feast day, but it isn't the one here. Verse 16 says Paul was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost. Antioch and Passover aren't part of this verse.
From Miletus, Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church. He's sailing past Ephesus, so he has them come to him. Funny how a man in a hurry still makes time for the people who matter.
Synagogue leaders aren't who Paul calls for here. Verse 17 says he sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church. Those are the people he wants to talk to before he sails on.
City officials would have a very different kind of meeting. But the text says Paul sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church. His business is with the church's leaders, not the city's.

explanations.answer: Publicly and from house to house
explanations.explanation: Paul says he taught them publicly and from house to house. That covers the big gatherings and the living rooms. He also says he did not shrink back from declaring anything that was helpful to them.
Letters and messengers are good tools, but that's not what Paul describes here. He says he taught them publicly and from house to house. He's talking about being right there with them.

explanations.answer: Outdoors and down by the riverside
explanations.explanation: A riverside lesson sounds lovely, but the text doesn't mention one. Paul says he taught publicly and from house to house. So think crowds and front doors.

explanations.answer: Repentance to God and faith in Jesus
explanations.explanation: Verse 21 says Paul was testifying “…about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.” That's the heart of what he told them. Turn to God, trust Jesus.

explanations.answer: Keeping the feasts and the law
explanations.explanation: Feasts and the law don't show up in what Paul says here. He says he was testifying about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Those two things were his message to Jews and Greeks alike.

explanations.answer: Fasting and giving to the poor
explanations.explanation: Giving does come up later in Paul's talk, but it isn't what he testified about here. In verse 21, he says he testified about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. That's the message he carried to everyone.

Paul says he was “…testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.” The word is alike, so the same message went to both. Nobody got a different version.
Paul actually says he was “…testifying to Jews and Greeks alike about repentance to God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.” So Greeks were included, not left out. Same message, both groups.
Paul says, “…in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me.” That's a lot of warnings. And he keeps heading toward Jerusalem anyway.
It's true, actually. Paul says, “…in town after town the Holy Spirit warns me that chains and afflictions await me.” It isn't one warning in one place. It happens in town after town.

explanations.answer: Finishing the ministry Jesus gave him
explanations.explanation: Paul says he considers his life of no value to himself, “…if only I may finish my course and complete the ministry I have received from the Lord Jesus…” That ministry is testifying to the good news of God's grace. With chains ahead, that's still the thing he wants most.

explanations.answer: Seeing his friends one more time
explanations.explanation: I bet Paul cares about these elders, but that's not what he names here. He says he wants to finish his course and complete the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus. In fact, a few verses later he tells them they won't see his face again (Acts 20:25).

Paul says he's going to Jerusalem not knowing what will happen to him there. He only knows that chains and afflictions await him. What matters to him is finishing his course and completing the ministry he received from the Lord Jesus.
It's the opposite, friend. Paul says, “Now I know that none of you among whom I have preached the kingdom will see my face again.” He isn't promising a return trip. He's saying goodbye.
Paul says, “Now I know that none of you among whom I have preached the kingdom will see my face again.” No return visit is promised. That sets up the tears at the end of this passage.
Paul says, “Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.” A flock needs someone who guards it and keeps it together. That's the job he hands these elders.
Builders is a fine word, but it isn't Paul's. He says, “Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.” Since he's been calling the church a flock, shepherds fits.
Judges isn't the word Paul uses. He tells the elders, “Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood.” He keeps the picture of a flock, and a flock gets shepherds.

Paul says, “I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock.” Wolves are the natural enemy of a flock, so he keeps his picture together. It's a warning, and he wants them awake for it.
Lions are scary, but they aren't Paul's word. He says savage wolves will come in among them and will not spare the flock. Since he's talking about a flock, wolves is the picture he paints.
A bear would be a big problem, but Paul doesn't mention one. He says, “I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock.” The word he picks is wolves.

explanations.answer: Distort the truth to draw disciples after them
explanations.explanation: Paul says those men will “…distort the truth to draw away disciples after them.” They twist the truth and gather followers for themselves. That's why he wants the elders alert.

explanations.answer: Leave the church and go their own way
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say they'll just walk away. He says men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them. The danger he names is twisted teaching, not quiet leaving.

explanations.answer: Hand the elders over to the rulers
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about rulers here. He says men from their own number will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them. The danger he names is twisted teaching.

explanations.answer: They can be built up and given an inheritance
explanations.explanation: Paul says the word of His grace “…can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are sanctified.” So the word does the building. And the inheritance is shared with all who are sanctified.

explanations.answer: They can be kept free from every hardship
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't promise that. He's just told them chains and afflictions await him (Acts 20:23). What he says the word of His grace can do is build them up and give them an inheritance among all who are sanctified.

explanations.answer: They can be given wealth and long lives
explanations.explanation: Wealth isn't what Paul offers. A few verses later he says he hasn't coveted anyone's silver or gold or clothing (Acts 20:33). The word of His grace can build them up and give them an inheritance among all who are sanctified.

Paul says, “…these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions.” He worked to provide for himself and his friends. I know a little about working with hands, though mine is a mustache.
That's close to the story, but it isn't the word. Paul says his own hands ministered to his needs and those of his companions. The work he points to is the work of his hands.
Family isn't what Paul points to here. He says, “…these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs and those of my companions.” The work came from his own hands.

explanations.answer: It is more blessed to give than to receive
explanations.explanation: Paul remembers “‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’…” He says it's by hard work like his that we must help the weak. Giving is the point.

explanations.answer: The worker is worthy of his wages
explanations.explanation: It's a good line about work, but it's not the one Paul remembers here. He recalls the words of the Lord Jesus Himself: “‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’…” Paul ties it to helping the weak through hard work.

explanations.answer: Ask and it will be given to you
explanations.explanation: Jesus does say those words (Matthew 7:7), but Paul doesn't use them here. In this passage he remembers “‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’…” That one fits with working hard to help the weak.
Verse 36 says Paul knelt down with all of them and prayed. After a long goodbye talk, he ends on his knees with them. No speeches this time.
Singing is a fine way to say goodbye, but the text doesn't mention it. It says Paul knelt down with all of them and prayed. That's what he does on his knees.
Paul has just finished a lot of talking, and no reading is mentioned. The text says he knelt down with all of them and prayed. That's the moment.
No tears held back here, friend. The text says, “They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him.” They wept openly, right there in front of everybody.
That's right. The text says, “They all wept openly as they embraced Paul and kissed him.” Nobody held anything back. I think this was a hard goodbye.
Verse 38 says they accompanied him to the ship. They'd prayed and wept together, and they still went with him there. I think nobody wanted to be the first to turn around.
The elders did come from Ephesus, but they don't head back yet. The text says they accompanied Paul to the ship. They stay with him right to the end.
Jerusalem is where Paul is headed, but that's not where the text says the elders go. It says they accompanied him to the ship. That's the place the passage names.
